_comment: EvercoatITWRD APP — Keycloak realm.
Imported on first start via --import-realm. Realm roles here MUST
match core.roles.code in 002_seed_roles_permissions.sql exactly.
A mismatch is silent: Keycloak issues a token with a role the
database has never heard of, the principal query returns no
permissions, and the user sees an empty application with no error.
tests/db/test_002_roles_permissions.py asserts the two lists agree.
Keycloak owns identity ONLY. It does not own authorization — roles
here are coarse bundles, and the application authorizes on
permissions read from the database (CLAUDE.md §6). Membership is
deliberately NOT a token claim: a JWT states identity, not current
authorization, so revoking a project membership must bite
immediately rather than whenever the access token expires.
_comment_tokens: Short access tokens because authorization is re-read from the
database each request anyway; a long-lived token buys nothing here
and widens the window on a stolen one. Refresh rotation is on, with
reuse detection, so a replayed refresh token invalidates the chain.
passwordPolicy: length(12) and notUsername(undefined) and notEmail(undefined) and upperCase(1) and lowerCase(1) and digits(1) and specialChars(1) and passwordHistory(5)

_comment: The web client is PUBLIC — a browser cannot keep a secret, and
shipping one would only create the illusion of confidentiality.
PKCE S256 is what actually protects the authorization code.
Redirect URIs are exact. A wildcard host here is an open redirect
and an authorization-code interception path. Adding a deployment
means adding its URI explicitly.
clients.name: EvercoatITWRD Web

protocolMappers._comment: Audience mapper. Without it the token's aud omits evercoat-api and the API rejects every request as invalid_audience — a failure that looks like a broken login.
protocolMappers.name: evercoat-api-audience

_comment: Bearer-only: the API validates tokens and never initiates a
login, so it needs no flows of its own.
It has NO service account. An API that can mint its own
privileged token has a path around the authorization chain, and
background work runs as the worker client instead.
clients.name: EvercoatITWRD API

_comment: Confidential client for Celery. Secret is a placeholder and is
replaced at provisioning from SOPS — it must never be the value
committed here.
The worker holds no realm role. Background jobs act on records
they are given, not on an identity that can approve anything.
clients.name: EvercoatITWRD Worker

_comment_users: No users are seeded here. Ten synthetic demo users — one per role —
are created by scripts/seed.sh, which labels them clearly as demo
data. Seeding users in a realm import means the same credentials
exist in every environment the file is imported into, including any
No default roles are assigned either: a new account should be able
to sign in and see nothing until someone deliberately grants it
